stemMd: Which of the following can most reasonably be inferred from the passage?

options.label: A
options.textMd: Nitrogen pollution has proved more harmful to lichens than sulphur dioxide ever was.

options.label: B
options.textMd: Sulphur dioxide is no longer released anywhere in Europe.

options.label: C
options.textMd: Lichens that have been driven out by sulphur dioxide cannot return.

options.label: D
options.textMd: A tree covered in lichens is not, on that fact alone, evidence that the air around it is clean.

options.label: E
options.textMd: Lichen surveys have become too expensive to be worth carrying out.

explanationMd:
Look for a fact in the text that undermines a natural assumption. The natural assumption is that plenty of lichens means clean air. The third paragraph says nitrogen-loving species, fed by vehicle exhausts and agricultural ammonia, "have spread at the expense of others", and that a tree in a clean-air city can be as crowded with lichens as a rural one "and yet be crowded with different ones". So a heavily covered tree may be covered by the very species that thrive on nitrogen pollution. The fourth paragraph adds that surveys must now read the make-up of the whole community. Together these imply that the amount of lichen on a tree does not, by itself, show that the air is clean.

Check the others. Sensitive lichens are said to have begun to return, so they can come back. The last paragraph says the method "is still cheap". Emissions are said to have fallen sharply in many European countries, which is not the same as stopping everywhere. And the passage never weighs the total harm done by nitrogen against that done by sulphur dioxide.

distractorRationale.a: Nitrogen favours some species and crowds out others, but the passage never compares its overall harm with that of sulphur dioxide, which once made many species vanish from cities.
distractorRationale.b: The passage says emissions fell sharply in many European countries. A sharp fall in many countries is not an end to emissions everywhere.
distractorRationale.c: The third paragraph says sensitive lichens began to return to city trees once emissions fell, though slowly and unevenly.
distractorRationale.e: The last paragraph says the method is still cheap; only what it measures has become more complicated.

accessibilityText: An inference question about the lichen passage. It asks which statement can most reasonably be inferred. The five choices: nitrogen pollution has proved more harmful to lichens than sulphur dioxide ever was; sulphur dioxide is no longer released anywhere in Europe; lichens driven out by sulphur dioxide cannot return; a tree covered in lichens is not, on that fact alone, evidence that the air around it is clean; lichen surveys have become too expensive to be worth carrying out.

provenance.notes: Original item written for this bank against an original passage. Every option is answerable, or refutable, from the passage text alone.

review.author: tolc-e-wave6-author

independentSolve.workingNotes: Nitrogen-loving species have spread, and the survey answer is now read from which species make up the community, not from how many lichens there are. So a lichen-covered tree does not by itself show clean air. A's comparison is never made. B contradicts 'fell sharply' (emissions dropped, they did not stop). C contradicts the return of sensitive lichens. E contradicts 'The method is still cheap'. [A second, separate blind solve (blind-reviewer-wave6-tolce-verbal-run2) reached the same answer: Paragraph 3 says nitrogen-loving species have spread and that a clean-air-city tree can be 'as crowded' with lichens as a country tree, but with different ones. So lichen cover alone does not show the air is clean; the mix of species has to be read. A is an unsupported comparison. B overreaches, since emissions only 'fell sharply in many' countries. C is contradicted, because sensitive lichens 'began to return'. E is contradicted, because 'The method is still cheap'.]

review.notes: Uniqueness check: the spread of nitrogen-loving species, and the need to read whole communities, support the correct choice. Three others are contradicted by the text and one asserts an unsupported comparison. Options were reordered after review to remove answer-position bias; ids and labels were remapped with the key.
